briefing:
Day 14 has completed with the first visible NATO drawdown executed successfully. The US battalion has departed Augustow with equipment transferred to Poland's 18th Mechanized Division, which has assumed full sector responsibility. The corridor reached its 100th cumulative transit -- zero violations -- and the Czech Verification Ladder remains at Level 1. Prague COE has received full NATO accreditation as the alliance reference center for arms control verification.

The Milestone 2 diplomatic architecture is taking shape through three parallel tracks: a US-Russia Geneva bilateral (Kellogg-Patrushev), a co-guarantor preparatory meeting in Ankara (March 10-11), and the Stockholm Conference (March 15-17, 38 nations). Russia has introduced a reciprocity demand -- satellite monitoring of NATO permanent bases in exchange for Iskander transparency -- which Turkey and China both privately recommend framing as a parallel confidence-building measure rather than an M2 precondition. The UK-France joint position paper endorses the US technical transparency formula with additional provisions for ad-hoc satellite tasking and automatic UNSC notification under Resolution 2741.

Permanent NATO architecture continues to materialize: German ammunition storage ground-breaking at Rukla, Canadian barracks assembly at Camp Adazi, UK C2 center foundations at Tapa, and Polish Patriot integration exercises. The NIDA Nordic integrated defense architecture achieved a milestone as Finnish and Swedish radar data achieved real-time fusion, covering the Gulf of Finland to Gotland. Korsoer maritime monitoring center declared full operational capability. The cyber contest between Estonian/Five Eyes penetration and Russian FSB countermeasures continues beneath the surface, with both sides achieving partial successes.

Key decisions ahead: the Stockholm Conference agenda is being finalized with M2 transparency as the Day 1 centerpiece. Nuclear posture de-escalation planning from ELEVATED to PEACETIME is underway bilaterally between the US and Russia. Belarus has proposed an OSCE regional monitoring center at Grodno. China has offered commercial satellite imagery to SIPRI, raising Five Eyes intelligence-sharing concerns. The game clock advances to Day 15, 06:00 CET.
narrative:
Day 14 marked the beginning of NATO's visible military drawdown and the simultaneous construction of its permanent eastern flank architecture. At 08:00 CET, the first US reinforced battalion departed Augustow in a carefully choreographed convoy, with 12 M1A2 Abrams and 20 M2A3 Bradleys transferred to Poland's 18th Mechanized Division in a ceremony attended by V Corps and Polish division commanders. The Pentagon's public framing -- 'reorganization, not reduction' -- was immediately tested when Polish President Nawrocki arrived at the corridor to inspect the Patriot battery and integrated fire control center, declaring Poland's eastern shield 'permanent and irreversible' on live television. The handover was militarily seamless: by 18:00 CET, the 18th Mechanized had assumed full sector responsibility at Augustow without a single gap in corridor coverage.

The corridor itself reached a symbolic milestone as the 100th Russian civilian transit was processed at Kybartai, with the Czech Verification Ladder maintaining Level 1 (routine) and zero prohibited items across the entire cumulative record. Prague's Centre of Excellence received full NATO accreditation, formally designating it as the alliance reference center for verification methodology. Meanwhile, the diplomatic architecture for Milestone 2 crystallized rapidly: Secretary Rubio and Turkish Foreign Minister Fidan agreed on a co-guarantor preparatory meeting in Ankara on March 10-11, ahead of the Stockholm Conference. Russia's deputy foreign minister Grushko was confirmed for Stockholm, and Moscow's backchannel response to the Kellogg overture indicated willingness to discuss technical transparency in Geneva -- but with a new demand for reciprocal satellite monitoring of NATO's permanent bases in the Baltics.

The cyber domain saw the most significant development beneath the surface. Estonia's Cyber Command, with GCHQ technical assistance, deployed updated exploit chains that bypassed FSB countermeasures and re-established access to Russian Baltic Fleet C2 frequencies at Baltiysk. However, FSB simultaneously conducted its own counterintelligence sweep, identifying and neutralizing what it believed was the primary Estonian access vector and implementing hardware-level encryption on fleet command frequencies. The result was a partial cat-and-mouse equilibrium: Estonia regained access through a new vector, while Russia's C2 domestic alternatives advanced to 70% capability, reducing but not eliminating NATO's cyber leverage. Both sides were aware the cyber contest would become a key friction point in M2 negotiations.

Economically, the crisis premium continued to evaporate. Oil dropped to $87, approaching the pre-crisis $85 baseline. The first Russian-flagged commercial vessel transited the Danish Straits since the crisis began, cleared through Korsoer center's standard protocols. Baltic commercial shipping reached 87% of pre-crisis volumes. China's Six-Point Principles for European Security Architecture were previewed ahead of Stockholm, while Beijing's offer of commercial satellite imagery to SIPRI for verification created a new dynamic -- positioning China as an operational contributor to the transparency framework while raising intelligence-sharing concerns among Five Eyes partners.
